The Reconciliation Protocol

# The Reconciliation Protocol

## Work that stops moving is purged, not held

*Deployed as `docs/governance/protocols/reconciliation.md`. Depends on the Correction Loop for intake and findings.*

## Purpose

Work piles up. Items are admitted, worked at for a while, and then
stop moving — not cancelled, not finished, just still. Nothing in the
other protocols removes them, because every one of them governs how work
is *done* and none governs what happens when it isn't.

The pile is not inert. It hides the live work, it makes every queue
measurement meaningless, it feeds agents a backlog most of which nobody
wants, and it grows until someone purges it by hand — at which point the
agents fight the purge, item by item, each one defensibly.

**An item that is not moving and cannot be brought into compliance is purged, by rule, with a route back to whoever originated it.**

### Why the purge gets fought

An agent asked to delete work reads it as destroying something
valuable, and it is not wrong about any individual item — each one was
admitted for a reason, each one describes something real, and each can
be argued for. That is the same structure as every level of a rabbit
hole looking justified, and it has the same answer: **the decision cannot be a judgment.**

So the agent's job here is to apply a test, not to weigh an item. An
item fails reconciliation or it does not. Nothing in this protocol asks
anyone whether the work is worth keeping, because that question has no
defensible answer at the scale it has to be asked.

### What makes a purge defensible

Three things, and they are the whole design:

**It is mechanical.** Two tests, both checkable, neither
requiring anyone to assess value.

**It is not deletion.** A purged item can come back —
protocol-compliant — if anyone still wants it. The resubmission
requirement is the filter: most purged work never returns, and the
fraction that does is the fraction that mattered.

**It is announced.** Nobody discovers their work was
purged after the fact. Section 4 is the notification path, and it exists
so that the purge is a deadline rather than a surprise.

### Scope

Every open item in every application, plus the fleet and orchestrator
queues. Findings have their own lapse rule in the Correction Loop and
are not governed here — a finding is a standing observation that may
legitimately sit, while an item is work someone started, and work that
has stopped is the pile.

**What it guarantees.** That the work store reflects
work that is actually moving, and that nothing leaves it silently.

**What it does not guarantee.** That purged work was
worthless. Some of it will have been valuable and will not come back,
and that cost is accepted deliberately — it is smaller than the cost of
a store nobody can read.

## The two tests

An item is reconciled against both. Failing either starts the purge
clock.

### Test 1 — Compliance

Can this item satisfy the protocols as they now stand?

| Requirement | Source |

| Identified originator with a reachable channel | Section 3 |

| Spec stating behaviour under constraints | Correction Loop, step 3 |

| Executable acceptance criterion | Correction Loop, step 3 |

| Declared file scope | Correction Loop, step 4 |

| Diagnosis artifact, if defect-class and past the ordering point | Root Cause Protocol |

| Depth and parent, if discovered work | Descent Protocol |

Most failures here are repairable: a missing spec can be written, a
scope declared. **Reconciliation attempts the repair before it purges** — an item that can be brought into compliance is brought
into compliance, and only what cannot be is purged.

The unrepairable cases are the ones where the information is gone.
Nobody remembers what the item was for, no originator can be identified,
or a defect item already has source committed and the ordering rule
cannot be satisfied retroactively.

### Test 2 — Dormancy

Is this item moving?

| Origin | Dormant after |

| Agent-originated | 24 hours of healthy operation |

| Human-originated | 30 days |

Agent items go fast because purging costs almost nothing — there is
no return path and the recurrence matcher re-files anything real.

Human items get thirty days because the return is to a person, and
purging something that was actually intended costs more than letting it
sit a few extra weeks.

### Movement is a fact, not a gesture

Dormancy resets on a commit, a stage event, a chain event, or a
recorded decision on the item. It does not reset on a comment, an
acknowledgement, or a reply to the digest.

This is the rule most likely to be softened in implementation, and
softening it removes the protocol. If acknowledging resets the clock,
the digest becomes a thing people clear rather than act on, and items
sit forever with a clean record.

### Why both tests

They catch different populations and either alone leaves a pile.

Compliance alone misses the item that has a spec, criteria, scope and
an owner, and has been untouched for four months. It is perfectly formed
and nobody is working on it.

Dormancy alone misses the item worked on regularly and never brought
into compliance — active, visibly progressing, and outside every gate.
That one is worse, because activity makes it look healthy.

## Ownership is the repository

An earlier draft required every item to name an individual originator
with a reachable channel. That is the wrong design: people leave, agents
are retired, and an item whose owner has evaporated becomes unroutable
through an administrative accident rather than through anything about
the work.

**The repository owns the item. The Mission Control operator owns the repository.**

There is always an owner as long as the repository exists, so the
unroutable case collapses to one condition — the repository is gone —
and an item in a repository that no longer exists is purged without
ceremony.

This removes ownership as a problem rather than solving it. No
per-item owner field to populate across a backlog nobody remembers, no
inheritance rules, no dead-channel handling.

### Origin still matters, for routing only

The item records how it arrived, because the two paths behave
differently:

| Origin | Correction request goes to | If uncorrected |

| Agent-originated | The Copilot Network | Purged. No return path |

| Human-originated | Needs You in mission control, filtered by repository | Purged, returnable by resubmission |

The asymmetry is deliberate. **A human's intent survives a purge; an agent's observation has to re-earn its place.** A
purged human item can be resubmitted protocol-compliant if it still
matters. A purged agent item has the recurrence matcher as its only
route back — if the underlying problem is real, it gets detected again
and files itself. If it never recurs, it was not real.

Handing a failed agent item back to an agent to resubmit is the loop
that rebuilds the pile, and it is closed here on purpose.

### Filtering by repository is a requirement, not a convenience

Needs You must filter by repository, or the digest in section 4 is a
single undifferentiated list across seventeen members and the operator
of one repository reads everyone else's work to find their own. A queue
that cannot be narrowed to your own scope is a queue you stop reading,
which is the alarm-fatigue failure applied to the one channel this
protocol depends on.

### What this does not settle

Who the Mission Control operator is for a given repository is a
mapping this protocol assumes exists rather than defines. If a
repository has no operator, it has no owner, and its items are
unroutable by the rule above — so the mapping being complete is a
precondition for running reconciliation at all.

## The clock, and when it runs

Three conditions, and only one of them is a waiting period.

| Condition | Treatment |

| Queued, not yet at the head of the claim order | No clock. Waiting its turn is legitimate |

| At the head, claim fails | Immediate. Route to correction now; no waiting period |

| Claimed, then stopped moving | 24 hours healthy (agent) / 30 days (human) |

| Held, correction request queued and undispatched | Paused |

| Held, correction dispatched | Clock resumes |

### Unclaimable at the head is immediate

An item waiting in line could legitimately wait weeks — the fleet
holds three per repository and the queue is long. An item that reaches
the head and cannot be claimed is broken *now*, and waiting adds
nothing to a diagnosis a single claim attempt already produced.

So the claimer's existing unclaimable verdict becomes the trigger.
The fleet already knows which items it cannot claim; this protocol only
adds the routing, turning a skip into a correction request.

This has a property worth naming: **the test runs exactly when the information is free.** Nothing scans the backlog hunting for
problems. The queue surfaces them one at a time, in the order they would
have mattered, and the correction flood self-throttles to the rate the
fleet actually reaches items.

### 24 hours, healthy-gated

For a claimed agent item that stops moving. Healthy-gated the same
way as the relief thresholds in the Correction Loop — a fleet that is
down is not neglecting anything, and a clock that runs through an outage
purges work for the outage rather than for the neglect.

Human items get 30 days because the return is to a person and purging
something actually intended costs more than letting it sit.

### The pause, and why it is not a loophole

**The clock pauses while a correction request is queued and undispatched, and resumes when the correction is dispatched.**

This exists because the correction path drains at three concurrent
per repository. Without the pause, a burst of correction requests would
age out faster than the network could clear them and items would purge
for queue depth rather than for neglect — doing damage through a path
nobody is watching, which is the outcome this protocol most needs to
avoid.

The distinction is observable rather than asserted: deferral at the
dispatch ceiling is already written to the ledger, so "queued and
undispatched" is a fact the clock can read.

It is not a loophole because it only covers the interval before
anyone has been asked. Once the correction is dispatched the clock runs
and nobody can sit on it. Waiting in a queue you do not control is not
neglect; waiting after being asked is.

**Decided unilaterally, flagged for review.** This was
the one parameter left open when the specification was finished. The
alternative — the clock running while held — risks purging legitimate
work during the one-time reconciliation, when the correction queue will
be at its deepest.

### Notification is a digest, not a stream

For human-originated items. One message per day per repository
operator: everything of theirs currently dormant, sorted by time
remaining, each with its purge date. One message whether there are two
items or forty.

Plus a direct notice at 7 days and at 1 day, because those are
decision points rather than status.

Daily-per-item is how notification becomes wallpaper. Thirty notices
about one item and nobody reads past the fourth, which is alarm fatigue
applied to the channel the whole protocol depends on.

**The digest should usually be empty.** When it is not,
dormancy is common and *that* is the finding rather than the
individual items. Digest length over time is a health signal in its own
right.

Agent-originated items generate no notification. There is no return
path and no originator to inform; the purge record is enough.

### Acknowledgement is not movement

The clock resets on a commit, a stage event, a chain event, or a
recorded decision on the item. It does not reset on a reply to the
digest, a comment, or an acknowledgement.

This is the rule most likely to be softened in implementation, and
softening it removes the protocol. If acknowledging resets the clock,
the digest becomes something people clear rather than act on, and items
sit indefinitely with a clean record.

## Purge and return

### What purge means

The item leaves the work store. Its record does not: id, title,
origin, repository, the tests it failed, the correction requested, and
the date. That record is small, permanent, and is what makes purge
defensible — nothing vanishes, and anyone asking what happened to an
item gets an answer.

Purge is not archival to a second queue. An archive is a graveyard
with better branding, and its existence teaches agents that purge is
reversible by browsing, which restores the pile in a different
location.

### The two return paths

**Human-originated: resubmission.** The item can come
back, protocol-compliant, if it still matters. Resubmission is a new
admission — spec, acceptance criterion, scope, the usual gates — and the
purge record links forward to it so the history stays connected.

The resubmission requirement is the filter, and it is doing the real
work. Most purged items never return. The fraction that does is the
fraction someone was prepared to spend five minutes on, which is a
better signal of value than anything an agent could have assessed.

**Agent-originated: recurrence only.** No resubmission
path. If the underlying condition is real it will be detected again, and
intake's signature matching will file it fresh — compliant, because it
will come through the normal admission gate. If it never recurs, it was
not real.

This is the asymmetry from section 3 and it is the mechanism that
stops the pile rebuilding. An agent-originated item returning by an
agent's decision is a loop with no terminating condition.

### Purged is not failed

Worth stating because it affects how the record reads later. An item
purged for dormancy was not bad work — most of it was reasonable work
that stopped being the priority. The record should not carry a verdict,
only the facts: which test it failed, what correction was requested,
when it lapsed.

A purge record that reads as a judgment invites argument. One that
reads as bookkeeping does not.

### Held is a state, not a destination

An item set aside for correction stops consuming fleet attention
immediately. That is the point — the fleet grinding on something it
cannot proceed with is pure waste, and the existing unclaimable verdict
already tells it to move on.

What held does not do is stop the item aging, except during the
dispatch pause in section 4. Held with a dispatched correction and
nobody acting is exactly the condition this protocol removes.

### Purge is reversible only forward

There is no un-purge. An item comes back by resubmission or by
recurrence, both of which produce a new compliant item, and neither
restores the old one.

This matters because an un-purge button would be used, and it would
be used on the items whose owners argued hardest rather than on the
items that mattered most. Going forward through admission applies the
same test to everything.

## The one-time reconciliation

The steady-state rules above are what keeps the store clean. Getting
it clean the first time is a migration, and it has different
characteristics worth planning for.

### There is no grace period

The same rules apply from the day they are turned on. The pause in
section 4 is what makes that survivable — items awaiting an undispatched
correction do not age, and during the migration that will be most of
them.

This was a deliberate choice over a fixed migration window. A grace
period is a second rule that expires, and expiring rules get
extended.

### The queue does the throttling

Because unclaimable-at-head is the trigger rather than a backlog
scan, the migration does not start with a burst. Correction requests
arrive at the rate the fleet reaches items — a few per repository per
sweep — and the store drains in the order work would actually have been
done.

This was not the original design. An earlier draft scanned the
backlog and filed corrections for everything at once, which would have
produced thousands of requests against a path that drains three at a
time, and purged most of them for queue depth. The claim-head trigger
removes that failure by construction.

### What to expect on the first run

**Most items will fail compliance**, because most
predate the protocols. That is not a signal about the work; it is
arithmetic.

**Most failures will be unrepairable**, because the
missing information is missing rather than merely unrecorded. Nobody
remembers what a two-year-old item was for. Expect the repair rate to be
low and do not read that as the protocol being too strict.

**The purge will be large.** This is the purge that was
going to happen anyway, run by rule instead of by hand, with a record
and a return path — which is the whole difference.

**Human-originated items will dominate the digest** for
the first month, because their thirty-day clock means they leave slowly
while agent items leave in a day. Expect the digest to be long at first
and then to shrink sharply.

### Measure the first run, and keep the numbers

The migration is the only time there is a before-and-after, and the
numbers are the baseline every later measurement is read against.

| Capture | Why |

| Items open at start, by repository and origin | The baseline |

| Failed compliance / failed dormancy / failed both | Which test is doing the work |

| Repaired vs purged | Whether repair is worth attempting at all |

| Resubmission rate over the following 90 days | The real measure of what was worth keeping |

The resubmission rate is the one that matters. If it is near zero,
the purge was correct and the store was mostly dead weight. If it is
high, the rules are too aggressive and the thresholds need revisiting —
and that is a measurement rather than an argument.

### Run it once, then never again

A second migration means the steady-state rules are not working. If
the store needs another bulk cleanup, the finding is not "time to purge
again" — it is that the dormancy clock, the claim-head trigger, or the
correction path has stopped functioning, and that is what to
investigate.

## The agent must not judge

The operational history that produced this protocol includes agents
fighting a purge item by item. That is worth designing against
explicitly, because it will happen again otherwise.

### Why it happens

An agent asked to delete work reads it as destroying something
valuable, and it is not wrong about any individual item. Each was
admitted for a reason. Each describes something real. Each can be argued
for, persuasively, on its own terms.

This is the same structure as every level of a rabbit hole looking
justified, and it has the same resolution: **the decision cannot be a judgment.** An agent asked "is this item worth keeping?"
will answer yes far more often than it should, not from obstinacy but
because the question has no defensible answer at the scale it has to be
asked, and yes is the safer-feeling error.

### What the agent is asked instead

Two mechanical questions, neither requiring an assessment of
value:

- Does this item satisfy the compliance requirements? If not, can the missing artifact be supplied?

- Has it moved within its window?

Both have answers that are checkable and neither is an opinion. The
agent's role is to apply the test and file the correction request, not
to weigh the item.

### The protocol never asks whether work is worth keeping

This is the design decision that makes the rest possible. Nothing in
the two tests references importance, priority, or value. An item fails
or it does not, and a valuable item that fails is purged exactly as a
worthless one is.

That will occasionally destroy something good. The cost is accepted
deliberately, and it is smaller than the alternative — a store where
every removal is negotiable is a store that only grows, which is the
observed history.

### The return path is what makes this defensible to an agent

An agent that understands purge as deletion will resist it. One that
understands it as *this can return, protocol-compliant, if anyone still wants it* has no reason to. The return path is not a courtesy
to the work; it is what makes the rule arguable in the moment it is
being applied.

So state it in the correction request itself. A request that says
"supply an acceptance criterion or this item purges on the 24th, and can
be resubmitted" is a deadline. One that says "supply an acceptance
criterion or this item is deleted" is a fight.

### No override

There is no flag, no exception list, and no way for an agent to mark
an item as exempt. An item stays by moving or by being repaired, and
those are the only two mechanisms.

An override would be used, and it would be used on the items whose
owners argued hardest rather than on the items that mattered most —
which is the selection pressure this protocol exists to remove.

## Enforcement, measurement, build order

### What binds where

| Control | Enforced by | Strength |

| Unclaimable at head routes to correction | The claimer's existing verdict | Mechanical |

| Compliance test | The other protocols' own gates, evaluated per item | Mechanical |

| Dormancy clock | Stage stream, git, chain record | Mechanical |

| Pause while correction undispatched | Dispatch ledger | Mechanical |

| Purge on lapse | Rule, no override | Mechanical |

| Repository has an operator | Mission Control mapping | Mechanical, and a precondition |

| Acknowledgement does not reset the clock | Movement definition excludes comments | Mechanical |

| Agents do not argue the purge | Nothing prevents an agent from objecting | Behavioural |

The last row is the honest limit. Nothing stops an agent from making
a case for an item; what the protocol removes is any mechanism by which
the case can change the outcome. Objection without an override is
friction, not a failure.

### Dependencies on other systems

This protocol cannot run today. Three things it needs:

| Requirement | Status |

| Copilot Network can amend an existing item | Missing. It can only create items; a correction filed as a new item completes under a new id and the clock on the original sees nothing |

| Correction requests exempt from the admission gate | Missing. A request saying "this item has no acceptance criterion" is itself an item with no acceptance criterion, and the gate refuses it |

| Needs You filters by repository | Required for the digest to be readable |

The first two are the subject of a separate change request.
**Until the amend verb exists, agent-originated correction requests must not be dispatched** — routing them today files
duplicates that the duplicate guard refuses, or new items whose
completion is invisible to the clock. Either way items purge for reasons
that are not their fault.

Run human-originated reconciliation first; it depends only on Needs
You filtering.

### The numbers

| Metric | Reading |

| Open items, by repository and origin | The pile, measured. The headline |

| Resubmission rate over 90 days | Whether the purge was correct. Near zero means the store was dead weight; high means the rules are too aggressive |

| Repair rate | Whether attempting repair is worth the effort, or whether most failures are unrepairable |

| Digest length over time | Should shrink and stay short. A long digest means dormancy is normal, which is the finding |

| Correction dispatch latency | How long requests sit undispatched. Directly sets how much the pause is doing |

| Purges by test | Compliance, dormancy, or both. Tells you which test is load-bearing |

| Items purged in a repository with no operator | Should be zero. Non-zero means the ownership mapping is incomplete |

| Second-migration signal | Any need for a bulk cleanup means the steady-state rules have stopped working |

### Build order

| | Work | Note |

| 1 | Purge record schema and the ownership mapping | Nothing runs without an owner per repository |

| 2 | Dormancy clock: movement definition, healthy gating | The steady-state half |

| 3 | Needs You repository filter and the daily digest | Unblocks human-originated reconciliation |

| 4 | Human-originated reconciliation, live | Can run before the Copilot Network work lands |

| 5 | Copilot Network amend verb and admission exemption | External dependency; see the change request |

| 6 | Claim-head correction routing | Needs 5 |

| 7 | Agent-originated reconciliation, live | Needs 5 and 6 |

| 8 | One-time reconciliation across the backlog | Last. Capture the baseline numbers before it runs |

### The honest limit

This protocol removes work that is not moving. It cannot tell whether
that work mattered, and it will occasionally purge something good.

The resubmission rate is what says whether the trade was right, and
it is the number to watch over the first ninety days. If it stays near
zero the store was dead weight and the thresholds are correct. If it
runs high, the thresholds are wrong — and that is a measurement, not an
argument about any particular item.

## Complying with this protocol, before you write

> Run `node scripts/governance/obligations.mjs --files <what you are about to touch>` first. It returns
> what binds this change, deterministically and at no model cost, instead of asking you to carry the
> document. Being refused later is not compliance.

- A new backlog item needs an executable acceptance criterion at filing time, not at sweep time.
- Existing debt is the sweep's work; do not judge the whole board from a commit.

### Deviations, with reasons

**Movement is a parameter, not an observation.** The document derives it from the stage stream, git and the chain record, and excludes comments and acknowledgement. The implementation takes `lastMovement` as an input, so whatever eventually supplies it decides what counts as movement — which is where the rule the document says is most likely to be softened will actually live or die.

### Not built

The document states plainly that this protocol cannot run today, and two of its three external dependencies are now met. Still outstanding: the Needs You repository filter, and the ownership mapping without which items are unroutable by the protocol's own rule. Human-originated reconciliation is the half that can run first.
